subChunks.title: Evidence Synthesis: Methods, Interpretation & Critical Evaluation
subChunks.hookHtml: In 2003, a meta-analysis of 39 randomised controlled trials concluded that antidepressants were significantly more effective than placebo for moderate-to-severe depression — a finding widely cited to justify prescribing. In 2008, a different meta-analysis of the same evidence base, by Irving Kirsch and colleagues, reached a dramatically different conclusion: when unpublished trials (held by drug companies) were included through Freedom of Information requests, the effect size for antidepressants over placebo fell below the threshold considered clinically significant. The gap between these conclusions was not a matter of different data — it was a matter of publication bias: only positive trials had been published, creating a systematically distorted evidence base that inflated apparent drug efficacy. This episode illustrates both the power and the vulnerability of evidence synthesis. A well-conducted systematic review, integrating all available evidence through transparent and reproducible methods, is the most reliable way to answer clinical and scientific questions at the population level. A poorly conducted or biased meta-analysis — whether through selective inclusion, inadequate quality assessment, or failure to account for publication bias — can produce confident, peer-reviewed conclusions that are demonstrably wrong. For a senior psychologist, the ability to critically appraise systematic reviews and understand the methodological conditions under which they can and cannot be trusted is not optional — it is the foundation of evidence-based practice.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Is a Systematic Review?

A systematic review is a structured synthesis of all available evidence on a specific research question, conducted according to a pre-registered protocol with explicit, reproducible search and selection methods. Unlike a narrative review, which reflects the reviewer's selective reading, a systematic review is designed to minimise selection bias through:

  • Pre-registration: Protocol registered before searches begin (PROSPERO, OSF) — prevents outcome switching and selective reporting
  • Comprehensive search: Multiple databases (PsycINFO, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane), grey literature, unpublished trials, conference abstracts
  • Explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria: Applied to identify eligible studies
  • Quality assessment: Systematic appraisal of included studies' risk of bias
  • Transparent reporting: PRISMA guidelines (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) specify what must be reported and how

Meta-Analysis: Statistical Synthesis

When systematic reviews include multiple quantitative studies measuring the same outcome, a meta-analysis can statistically synthesise their results into an overall estimate — typically an effect size.

Common effect size measures:

Cohen's d         — standardised mean difference between groups;
                   .2 = small, .5 = medium, .8 = large
Odds ratio (OR)   — ratio of odds of outcome in treatment vs. control
Risk ratio (RR)   — ratio of risk of outcome in treatment vs. control
Correlation (r)   — strength of relationship between variables;
                   .1 = small, .3 = medium, .5 = large

Weighting: Larger studies (with smaller standard errors) are given more weight in the meta-analytic synthesis, producing a weighted average effect size.

Heterogeneity: I² statistic quantifies the proportion of total variability in effect sizes attributable to between-study heterogeneity rather than chance. High heterogeneity (I² >75%) signals that studies are not measuring the same effect — pooling them may be methodologically inappropriate. Heterogeneity should be investigated through subgroup analyses and meta-regression, not ignored.

Fixed vs. random effects models: Fixed effects models assume all studies estimate the same underlying effect; random effects models assume studies estimate a distribution of effects. Given that psychological interventions vary across studies in populations, settings, and treatment delivery, random effects models are usually more appropriate.

Publication Bias and Its Correction

Publication bias is the systematic tendency for studies with positive or significant results to be published at higher rates than studies with null or negative results. Its consequences for meta-analysis are severe: if only positive studies are published, the meta-analytic effect size estimate is inflated.

Detection methods:

  • Funnel plots: Plots of effect size against standard error. In the absence of bias, studies should form a symmetrical funnel shape; asymmetry suggests publication bias or small-study effects.
  • Egger's test: Statistical test for funnel plot asymmetry
  • Fail-safe N: Estimates how many null studies would need to exist unpublished to reduce the meta-analytic effect to non-significance
  • Trim and fill: Imputes missing studies to produce a bias-corrected effect size estimate

The Kirsch antidepressants meta-analysis demonstrated that accessing unpublished trials through regulatory agencies (FDA) can dramatically change conclusions. The Open Science movement's push for pre-registration of studies directly addresses this: if trials are registered before data collection, the number of registered but unpublished trials can be identified.

Quality Assessment of Primary Studies

The quality of a meta-analysis is limited by the quality of the studies it includes. Systematic reviews use structured tools to assess risk of bias:

Cochrane RoB 2      — randomised controlled trials; assesses:
                      allocation concealment, blinding, missing
                      data, selective reporting

ROBINS-I            — non-randomised studies

QUADAS-2            — diagnostic accuracy studies

NOS (Newcastle-     — cohort and case-control studies
Ottawa Scale)

Studies rated as high risk of bias should be given less weight in conclusions, or sensitivity analyses should be conducted excluding high-bias studies to test whether results change.

Interpreting and Applying Systematic Review Evidence

Statistical significance is not clinical significance. A statistically significant effect size of d = 0.2 (small) may be detectable at large sample sizes but clinically trivial — not worth the cost, risk, or time of treatment. Conversely, a clinically meaningful effect in a small, imprecise study may not reach statistical significance. The GRADE framework (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations) provides a structured approach to rating the certainty of evidence and translating it into clinical recommendations, explicitly distinguishing the strength of evidence from the strength of the recommendation.

Systematic reviews answer questions about average effects in studied populations — they do not directly answer questions about individual patients. Moderator analyses (examining whether effect sizes differ by patient characteristics) and subgroup analyses can provide more clinically specific guidance, but are prone to spurious findings when not pre-specified.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen projects two forest plots on the screen — the same treatment, the same question, but very different effect size estimates. 'Both of these are published, peer-reviewed meta-analyses,' she says. 'They reach contradictory conclusions. How do you decide which one to believe?'

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: A systematic review is not the same as a good systematic review. The label confers authority in a way that the methodology may not deserve. Publication bias, selective inclusion, inadequate quality assessment, high heterogeneity pooled inappropriately — any of these can produce a meta-analysis that has the appearance of rigorous synthesis and the substance of noise. Your job as a senior psychologist is not to take the conclusion at face value. Your job is to look at the forest plot, examine the funnel plot, find the heterogeneity statistics, and ask: would I make a clinical recommendation on the basis of this evidence? And if not, why not?

storyBeats.speaker: The antidepressant publication bias case
storyBeats.text: Turner et al. (2008) compared published antidepressant trial data against the full FDA registry of registered trials. Of 74 registered trials, 38 showed positive results — of which 37 were published. Of 36 trials showing negative or questionable results, only 14 were published; the rest were either not published or published as showing positive results through selective outcome reporting. When Turner et al. conducted a meta-analysis including all registered trials, the effect size fell from d = 0.41 (published-only) to d = 0.31 — a clinically relevant reduction. This represents one of the most important methodological demonstrations in psychiatry: the published evidence base can systematically overestimate effects by a substantial margin when publication bias is present and unpublished trials are excluded.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: I want you to understand that knowing the methods does not make you cynical about evidence — it makes you discriminating. A well-conducted, pre-registered, publication-bias-corrected meta-analysis with low heterogeneity and high-quality primary studies is genuinely the best available guide to what works. The problem is not evidence synthesis — the problem is evidence synthesis done badly. Your job is to tell the difference.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
You are reviewing a published meta-analysis examining the effectiveness of mindfulness-based interventions (MBI) for reducing anxiety. The meta-analysis reports: 28 randomised controlled trials included (N = 1,843 participants total); overall effect size d = 0.68 (p < .001); I² = 78%; funnel plot shows marked asymmetry with several small positive studies at the top; subgroup analysis shows larger effects in studies with <50 participants (d = 0.89) compared to studies with >100 participants (d = 0.41).

  1. What does the I² value of 78% tell you about this meta-analysis, and what implications does it have for interpreting the overall effect size estimate?
  2. What does funnel plot asymmetry combined with the subgroup result (small studies showing larger effects) suggest about the validity of the overall effect size?
  3. Given these findings, what level of certainty would you assign to the conclusion that MBIs are moderately effective for anxiety (d = 0.68), and what would you recommend for clinical decision-making?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. I² of 78%: I² quantifies the proportion of total variability in effect sizes attributable to between-study heterogeneity rather than chance sampling variation. An I² of 78% is very high by conventional thresholds (typically: <25% = low, 25–50% = moderate, >75% = high heterogeneity). This means 78% of the variability in effect size estimates across the 28 studies is explained by real differences between studies — in populations, intervention content and delivery, outcome measurement, comparison conditions, etc. — rather than random sampling variability. The implication is serious: pooling the studies into a single overall effect size estimate is methodologically questionable. A single d = 0.68 conceals the fact that some studies show much larger effects and others show much smaller ones (or potentially null effects), and the differences between studies are systematic, not random. The overall estimate may not accurately represent the effect of any particular mindfulness intervention in any particular context. The heterogeneity should be investigated through subgroup and meta-regression analyses to identify what moderates the effect, rather than reported as a single combined estimate.

2. Funnel plot asymmetry + small-study effect: Funnel plot asymmetry, where small positive studies are overrepresented at the top of the plot, is a signature pattern of publication bias combined with small-study effects. The subgroup result dramatically confirms this concern: large studies (>100 participants) show an effect of d = 0.41 (small to moderate), while small studies (<50 participants) show d = 0.89 (large). This pattern is not consistent with a genuine moderating effect of sample size — it is consistent with: (a) publication bias, where small studies with null or small effects were not published (only small studies with impressive results made it through); and (b) small-study bias more broadly, where small studies with poorer methodology inflate effect sizes. The 'true' effect, accounting for these biases, is likely much closer to the large-study estimate of d = 0.41 — if that much — than to the uncorrected pooled estimate of d = 0.68.

3. Certainty and clinical recommendation: Given the high heterogeneity (making the pooled estimate uninterpretable), marked publication bias and small-study effects (inflating the estimate), and the discrepancy between small and large study estimates, this meta-analysis provides only low certainty evidence that MBIs have a moderate effect on anxiety. Using the GRADE framework, the evidence would be rated down from RCT-level starting point due to: inconsistency (high heterogeneity, I² = 78%); suspected publication bias (asymmetric funnel plot, small-study effects). A GRADE rating of Low or Moderate certainty would be appropriate. Clinical recommendation: MBIs should not be recommended with high confidence based on this evidence. Clinicians should be cautious about applying the d = 0.68 figure to clinical decision-making; the more credible estimate from large, better-powered studies is d = 0.41 — a small to moderate effect. The appropriate recommendation is: MBIs may offer modest anxiety reduction, particularly when combined with other interventions; more large, rigorously conducted, pre-registered trials are needed. Publication bias should be addressed through prospective trial registration and data sharing requirements.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A NICE guideline committee is considering recommending a new psychological intervention based on a meta-analysis showing d = 0.55 with 95% CI [0.42, 0.68], p < .001. The meta-analysis included 15 RCTs, I² = 35%, no evidence of funnel plot asymmetry, and all studies were rated low risk of bias using Cochrane RoB 2. Critically evaluate the quality of this evidence and what additional considerations the committee should weigh in deciding whether to recommend the intervention. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
This meta-analysis presents meaningfully stronger evidence than typical in the field. The I² of 35% (moderate heterogeneity) indicates moderate but not excessive between-study variability — pooling is more defensible than in high-heterogeneity situations, though sources of heterogeneity should still be explored. Absence of funnel plot asymmetry reduces (though does not eliminate) concern about publication bias. Low risk of bias across all 15 RCTs using Cochrane RoB 2 — the most stringent current risk of bias tool — substantially increases confidence in the primary evidence. The 95% CI excludes zero with a reasonably tight range [0.42, 0.68], suggesting the effect estimate is fairly precise.

Using GRADE, this evidence would tentatively be rated Moderate to High certainty — higher than most psychological intervention meta-analyses, which typically include some high-bias studies and show heterogeneity.

Additional considerations for the guideline committee: (1) Clinical significance — d = 0.55 is medium by Cohen's conventions, but the committee should assess whether this translates to clinically meaningful improvement for patients, using responder rates and measures of functional recovery rather than standardised mean differences alone. (2) Population applicability — were trial populations representative of the patients who will receive the intervention in routine NHS care? RCT populations are often more selected than clinical reality. (3) Cost-effectiveness — the intervention may be effective but not cost-effective relative to existing options; NICE requires health economic analysis. (4) Implementation — effective in trials does not guarantee effective when rolled out at scale with typical workforce training.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what a forest plot is and how a meta-analysis combines results from many different studies into one conclusion — and why that conclusion might still be wrong.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The systematic tendency for studies with positive or significant results to be published at higher rates than null or negative studies, creating a biased literature. A major threat to the validity of meta-analytic conclusions; mitigated by trial pre-registration and open data requirements.

A measure of heterogeneity in meta-analysis: the proportion of total variability in effect sizes attributable to between-study differences (true heterogeneity) rather than sampling error. Values >75% indicate high heterogeneity that may make pooling questionable.

Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluations — a structured system for rating the certainty of evidence (high, moderate, low, very low) and translating it into clinical recommendations. Widely used by NICE, WHO, and Cochrane.

A graph plotting effect size against standard error for studies in a meta-analysis. Symmetrical shape indicates no publication bias; asymmetry (particularly small positive studies at the top) suggests publication bias or small-study effects inflating the overall estimate.

questions.questionHtml: In a meta-analysis, what does an I² value of 78% indicate?
options: 78% of the included studies showed positive effects
78% of the total variability in effect sizes is attributable to between-study heterogeneity rather than chance sampling variation
The meta-analysis included 78% of all relevant studies
78% of the sample met diagnostic criteria for the condition under study
questions.correctAnswer: 78% of the total variability in effect sizes is attributable to between-study heterogeneity rather than chance sampling variation
questions.explanationHtml: I² is a measure of statistical heterogeneity in meta-analysis. It quantifies what proportion of the total variability in effect sizes across studies is attributable to true between-study differences (heterogeneity) rather than expected sampling variation. I² of 78% is high (conventional thresholds: <25% = low; 25–50% = moderate; >75% = high), suggesting that most of the variability between studies reflects real differences — in populations, intervention content, outcome measurement, etc. — rather than random fluctuation. This has important implications: it means a single pooled effect size estimate may not accurately represent any particular study's intervention in any particular context, and the sources of heterogeneity should be investigated before drawing clinical conclusions.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: A statistically significant effect size in a meta-analysis (p < .001) is sufficient to conclude that an intervention is clinically meaningful and should be recommended for routine practice.
questions.explanationHtml: False. Statistical significance and clinical significance are distinct. With large combined sample sizes in meta-analysis, even very small effect sizes may reach statistical significance (p < .001) while being clinically trivial. A d = 0.15, for example, might be highly statistically significant in a large meta-analysis but represent a difference unlikely to be perceptible to patients or affect functional outcomes meaningfully. The GRADE framework explicitly requires evaluation of both statistical precision and clinical significance before formulating recommendations. Additional considerations for clinical recommendation include: cost-effectiveness, comparison with existing treatments, applicability of trial populations to clinical practice, and implementation feasibility. Statistical significance is necessary but far from sufficient for evidence-based clinical recommendation.

questions.questionHtml: A meta-analysis of psychotherapy for depression reports d = 0.82 overall, but the funnel plot is markedly asymmetric and subgroup analysis shows d = 0.45 in large studies (>100 participants) versus d = 1.1 in small studies (<30 participants). A colleague argues 'the overall effect size is convincing — d = 0.82 is large.' What is the most accurate evaluation of this argument?
options: Correct — large effect sizes are always clinically meaningful regardless of heterogeneity

The argument ignores strong evidence of publication bias and small-study effects that are inflating the overall estimate; the more credible effect size is likely closer to the large-study estimate of d = 0.45
The argument is correct because d = 0.82 accounts for all available evidence including small studies
The argument should be accepted because statistical significance validates the overall effect size
questions.correctAnswer: The argument ignores strong evidence of publication bias and small-study effects that are inflating the overall estimate; the more credible effect size is likely closer to the large-study estimate of d = 0.45
questions.explanationHtml: The pattern described — funnel plot asymmetry plus substantially larger effect sizes in small studies compared to large ones — is the signature of publication bias and small-study effects. Small studies with null results are not published; only small studies with large, impressive effects make it into the literature. Large studies, which have greater statistical power and are more often conducted with adequate methodological rigour, provide less biased estimates. The systematic discrepancy between small-study and large-study estimates is not explained by a genuine moderating effect of sample size — it reflects bias. The uncorrected pooled estimate of d = 0.82 is inflated by the overrepresentation of biased small studies. The more defensible estimate is d = 0.45 — itself possibly still subject to bias. The colleague's argument at face value ignores the fundamental threats to validity that the methodological indicators reveal.
